nameStory: This lichen is named after someone named Langdon, though the specific person honored by this scientific name is lost to botanical history. The genus name Heterodermia means 'different skin' in Greek, referring to how these lichens have distinctly different-colored upper and lower surfaces that create a two-toned appearance.
description: Langdon's Fringe Lichen is a leafy, crusty organism that's actually two living things working together - a fungus and an algae. It forms small, grayish patches on tree bark and rocks, spreading outward in overlapping lobes that look a bit like tiny lettuce leaves. Individual patches typically grow 1-3 inches across, though several can merge to cover larger areas. Like all lichens, it grows extremely slowly, adding just millimeters each year.

idTips.label: Lobed edges
idTips.description: The outer edges are divided into distinct finger-like lobes that feel papery-thin and slightly brittle when dry, becoming more flexible when damp

idTips.label: Two-toned coloring
idTips.description: Upper surface is pale gray to whitish, while the undersurface is distinctly darker brown to black, creating a striking contrast when lobes curl up

idTips.label: Powdery texture
idTips.description: Surface often has a slightly powdery or frosted appearance that may rub off on your fingers with gentle touching

idTips.label: Bark attachment
idTips.description: Attaches loosely to bark with small root-like structures, allowing edges to lift and curl away from the surface

idTips.label: Size and growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms small to medium patches that spread outward in a roughly circular pattern, with newer growth at the edges appearing lighter colored

habitat: This rare lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring older oaks, maples, and hickories in mature forests. It prefers trees with rough, furrowed bark in areas with good air quality, typically at low to moderate elevations throughout New England. Look for it in old-growth or second-growth forests where the canopy provides filtered light but isn't too dense.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after winter moisture has kept the lichen hydrated and pliable, making the lobed structure easier to see and the colors more vibrant.
seasonality.summer: May appear more dried and brittle during hot, dry periods, with edges curling more noticeably and colors appearing more muted or grayish.
seasonality.fall: Good time for observation as falling leaves expose more trunk surface, and autumn moisture keeps the lichen in good condition for identification.
seasonality.winter: Often well-hydrated from snow and rain, showing its best colors and most flexible texture, though may be obscured by snow on lower trunks.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once by citizen scientists, making it rarer than many endangered animals - you're more likely to see a wild moose than find this tiny gray organism!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other fringe lichens, but the combination of its small size, distinctly two-toned coloring, and loose attachment to bark helps distinguish it. Remember: 'Langdon's lifts' - the edges tend to curl up and lift away from the bark more than similar species.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means any sighting would be scientifically significant - always photograph suspected finds and consider reporting them to local naturalist groups or iNaturalist for expert verification.
compareHints: Unlike the more common Powdered Fringe Lichen which tends to be larger and more densely powdery, Langdon's Fringe Lichen is smaller with less prominent powdery coating. It differs from Obscure Shield Lichen by having more distinct lobing and the characteristic loose attachment that allows edges to lift from the substrate. The two-toned coloring is generally more pronounced than in its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative the Obscure Shield Lichen, Powdered Fringe Lichen has obvious white powdery patches and more pronounced fringe along the lobe edges.
Unlike Powdered Fringe Lichen which has a chalky, powdery surface coating, Casaretto's Fringe Lichen has a cleaner, smoother upper surface.
Unlike its relative the Powdered Fringe Lichen which has obvious white powdery patches, Obscure Shield Lichen lacks any powdery coating and has a much more uniform, smooth crusty surface.
